{{Short description|Ensemble of states at constant pressure}}
{{Statistical mechanics|cTopic=[[Statistical ensemble (mathematical physics)|Ensembles]]}}

The '''isothermal–isobaric ensemble''' (constant temperature and constant pressure ensemble) is a [[Statistical ensemble (mathematical physics)|statistical mechanical ensemble]] that maintains constant temperature <math>T \,</math> and constant pressure <math>P \,</math> applied. It is also called the <math>NPT</math>-ensemble, where the number of particles <math>N \,</math> is also kept as a constant.  This ensemble plays an important role in chemistry as chemical reactions are usually carried out under constant pressure condition.<ref name="dill">{{cite book |last1=Dill |first1=Ken A. |last2=Bromberg |first2=Sarina |last3=Stigter |first3=Dirk |title=[[Molecular Driving Forces]] |year=2003 |publisher=[[Garland Science]] |location=New York}}</ref> The NPT ensemble is also useful for measuring the equation of state of model systems whose [[virial expansion]] for pressure cannot be evaluated, or systems near first-order [[Phase transition|phase transitions]].<ref name="frenkel">{{cite book |last1=Frenkel |first1=Daan. |last2=Smit |first2=Berend |title=[[Understanding Molecular Simluation]] |year=2002 |publisher=[[Academic Press]] |location=New York}}</ref>

In the ensemble, the probability of a [[Microstate (statistical mechanics)|microstate]] <math>i</math> is <math>Z^{-1}e^{-\beta(E_i + pV_i)}</math>, where <math>Z</math> is the [[Partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]], <math>E_i</math> is the internal energy of the system in microstate <math>i</math>, and <math>V_i</math> is the volume of the system in microstate <math>i</math>.

The probability of a macrostate is <math>Z^{-1}e^{-\beta(E + pV - TS)} = Z^{-1}e^{-\beta G}</math>, where <math>G</math> is the [[Gibbs free energy]].

==Derivation of key properties==

The partition function for the <math>NpT</math>-ensemble can be derived from [[statistical mechanics]] by beginning with a system of <math>N</math> identical atoms described by a [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] of the form <math>\mathbf{p}^2/2m+U(\mathbf{r}^n)</math> and contained within a box of volume <math>V=L^3</math>. This system is described by the partition function of the [[canonical ensemble]] in 3 dimensions:

<math display="block">Z^\text{sys}(N, V, T) = \frac{1}{\Lambda^{3N} N!} \int_0^L \cdots \int_0^L d\mathbf{r}^N \exp\left[-\beta U{\left(\mathbf{r}^N\right)}\right] ,</math>

where <math display="inline">\Lambda = \sqrt{h^2 \beta/(2 \pi m)} </math>, the [[thermal de Broglie wavelength]] (<math>\beta = 1 / k_\text{B} T  </math> and <math>k_\text{B}</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]), and the factor <math>1/N!</math> (which accounts for indistinguishability of particles) both ensure normalization of entropy in the quasi-classical limit.<ref name="frenkel"/> It is convenient to adopt a new set of coordinates defined by <math> L \mathbf{s}_i = \mathbf{r}_i </math> such that the partition function becomes

<math display="block">Z^\text{sys}(N, V, T) = \frac{V^N}{\Lambda^{3N} N!} \int_0^1 \cdots \int_0^1 d\mathbf{s}^N \exp\left[-\beta U{\left(\mathbf{s}^N\right)}\right].</math>

If this system is then brought into contact with a bath of volume <math>V_0</math> at constant temperature and pressure containing an [[ideal gas]] with total particle number <math>M</math> such that <math>M-N \gg N</math>, the partition function of the whole system is simply the product of the partition functions of the subsystems:

<math display="block">Z^\text{sys+bath}(N, V, T) = \frac{V^N(V_0-V)^{M-N}}{\Lambda^{3M} N!(M-N)!} \int d\mathbf{s}^{M-N} \int d\mathbf{s}^N \exp\left[-\beta U{\left(\mathbf{s}^N\right)}\right] .</math>

[[File:Constant_pressure_system_immersed_in_a_constant_temperature_bath.png|thumb|right|The system (volume <math>V</math>) is immersed in a much larger bath of constant temperature, and closed off such that particle number remains fixed. The system is separated from the bath by a piston that is free to move, such that its volume can change.]]

The integral over the <math>\mathbf{s}^{M-N}</math> coordinates is simply <math>1</math>. In the limit that <math>V_0 \to \infty</math>, <math>M \to \infty</math> while <math>(M-N)/V_0=\rho</math> stays constant, a change in volume of the system under study will not change the pressure <math>p</math> of the whole system. Taking <math>V/V_0 \to 0</math> allows for the approximation <math>(V_0-V)^{M-N} = V_0^{M-N} (1-V/V_0)^{M-N} \approx V_0^{M-N} \exp[-(M-N)V/V_0] </math>. For an ideal gas, <math>(M-N)/V_0 = \rho = \beta P</math> gives a relationship between density and pressure. Substituting this into the above expression for the partition function, multiplying by a factor <math>\beta P</math> (see below for justification for this step), and integrating over the volume V then gives

<math display="block">\Delta^\text{sys+bath}(N, P, T) = \frac{\beta P V_0^{M-N}}{\Lambda^{3M}N!(M-N)!}\int dV \, V^N e^{-\beta P V} \int d\mathbf{s}^N e^{-\beta U(\mathbf{s})} .</math>

The partition function for the bath is simply <math>\Delta^\text{bath}=V_0^{M-N}/[(M-N)!\Lambda^{3(M-N)}</math>. Separating this term out of the overall expression gives the partition function for the <math>NpT</math>-ensemble:

<math display="block">\Delta^\text{sys}(N, P, T) = \frac{\beta P}{\Lambda^{3N}N!} \int dV \, V^N e^{-\beta P V} \int d\mathbf{s}^N e^{-\beta U(\mathbf{s})} .</math>

Using the above definition of <math>Z^\text{sys}(N,V,T)</math>, the partition function can be rewritten as

<math display="block">\Delta^\text{sys}(N, P, T) = \beta P \int dV \, e^{-\beta P V} Z^\text{sys}(N, V, T) ,</math>

which can be written more generally as a weighted sum over the partition function for the canonical ensemble

<math display="block">\Delta(N, P, T) = \int Z(N, V, T) \,e^{-\beta P V} C \, dV. </math>

The quantity <math>C</math> is simply some constant with units of inverse volume, which is necessary to make the integral [[dimensionless quantity|dimensionless]]. In this case, <math>C=\beta P</math>, but in general it can take on multiple values. The ambiguity in its choice stems from the fact that volume is not a quantity that can be counted (unlike e.g. the number of particles), and so there is no “natural metric” for the final volume integration performed in the above derivation.<ref name="frenkel"/> This problem has been addressed in multiple ways by various authors,<ref name="Attard">{{cite journal |last1=Attard |first1= Phil |date= 1995|title= On the density of volume states in the isobaric ensemble|journal= [[Journal of Chemical Physics]]|volume=103 |issue=24 |pages=9884–9885 |doi=10.1063/1.469956|bibcode= 1995JChPh.103.9884A }}</ref><ref name="Koper">{{cite journal |last1=Koper |first1= Ger J. M. |last2=Reiss |first2=Howard |date= 1996|title= Length Scale for the Constant Pressure Ensemble: Application to Small Systems and Relation to Einstein Fluctuation Theory |journal= [[Journal of Physical Chemistry]]|volume=100 |issue=1 |pages=422–432 |doi=10.1021/jp951819f}}</ref> leading to values for C with the same units of inverse volume. The differences vanish (i.e. the choice of <math>C</math> becomes arbitrary) in the [[thermodynamic limit]], where the number of particles goes to infinity.<ref name="hill">{{cite book |last1=Hill |first1=Terrence |title= Statistical Mechanics: Principles and Selected Applications |year=1987 |publisher = [[Dover Publications|Dover]] |location=New York}}</ref>

The <math>NpT</math>-ensemble can also be viewed as a special case of the Gibbs canonical ensemble, in which the [[microstate (statistical mechanics)|macrostates]] of the system are defined according to external temperature <math>T</math> and external forces acting on the system <math>\mathbf{J}</math>. Consider such a system containing <math>N</math> particles. The Hamiltonian of the system is then given by <math>\mathcal{H}-\mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{x}</math> where <math>\mathcal{H}</math> is the system's Hamiltonian in the absence of external forces and <math>\mathbf{x}</math> are the [[conjugate variables (thermodynamics)|conjugate variables]] of <math>\mathbf{J}</math>. The microstates <math>\mu</math> of the system then occur with probability defined by <ref name="kardar">{{cite book |last1=Kardar |first1=Mehran |title=Statistical Physics of Particles |year=2007 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=New York}}</ref>

<math display="block">p(\mu,\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{Z}} \exp\left[-\beta \mathcal{H}(\mu) + \beta \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{x}\right]</math>

where the normalization factor <math>\mathcal{Z}</math> is defined by

<math display="block">\mathcal{Z}(N, \mathbf{J}, T) = \sum_{\mu,\mathbf{x}} \exp[- \beta \mathcal{H}(\mu) + \beta \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{x}].</math>

This distribution is called [[Boltzmann distribution#Generalized Boltzmann distribution|generalized Boltzmann distribution]] by some authors.<ref name="Gao2019">{{cite journal |last1= Gao |first1= Xiang |last2= Gallicchio |first2= Emilio |first3= Adrian |last3= Roitberg  |date= 2019 |title= The generalized Boltzmann distribution is the only distribution in which the Gibbs-Shannon entropy equals the thermodynamic entropy | url = https://aip.scitation.org/doi/abs/10.1063/1.5111333 | journal = The Journal of Chemical Physics | volume = 151 | issue = 3 | pages = 034113 | doi = 10.1063/1.5111333 | pmid = 31325924 | arxiv = 1903.02121 | bibcode = 2019JChPh.151c4113G |s2cid= 118981017 |access-date= }}</ref>

The <math>NpT</math>-ensemble can be found by taking <math>\mathbf{J} = -P</math> and <math>\mathbf{x} = V</math>. Then the normalization factor becomes

<math display="block">\mathcal{Z}(N, \mathbf{J}, T) = \sum_{\mu, \{\mathbf{r}_i\} \in V} \exp\left[-\beta \left(P V + \frac{\mathbf{p}^2}{2m} + U{\left(\mathbf{r}^N\right)}\right)\right] , </math>

where the Hamiltonian has been written in terms of the particle momenta <math>\mathbf{p}_i</math> and positions <math>\mathbf{r}_i</math>. This sum can be taken to an integral over both <math>V</math> and the microstates <math>\mu</math>. The measure for the latter integral is the standard measure of [[phase space]] for [[identical particles]]: <math>\textrm{d} \Gamma_N = \frac{1}{h^3N!}\prod_{i=1}^N d^3\mathbf{p}_i d^3\mathbf{r}_i</math>.<ref name="kardar"/> The integral over <math>\exp(-\beta \mathbf{p}^2/2m)</math> term is a [[Gaussian integral]], and can be evaluated explicitly as

<math display="block"> \int \prod_{i=1}^N \frac{d^3\mathbf{p}_i}{h^3}\exp\bigg[-\beta \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{p^2_i}{2m}\bigg] = \frac{1}{\Lambda^{3N}} .</math>

Inserting this result into <math>\mathcal{Z}(N,P,T)</math> gives a familiar expression:<ref name="kardar"/>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\mathcal{Z}(N, P, T) &= \frac{1}{\Lambda^{3N}N!} \int dV e^{-\beta P V} \int d\mathbf{r}^N e^{-\beta U(\mathbf{r})} \\[1ex]
&= \int dV \, e^{-\beta P V} Z(N, V, T) .
\end{align}</math>

This is almost the partition function for the <math>NpT</math>-ensemble, but it has units of volume, an unavoidable consequence of taking the above sum over volumes into an integral. Restoring the constant <math>C</math> yields the proper result for <math>\Delta(N, P, T)</math>.

From the preceding analysis it is clear that the characteristic state function of this ensemble is the [[Gibbs free energy]],

<math display="block">G(N, P, T) = - k_\text{B} T \ln \Delta(N, P, T) </math>

This [[thermodynamic potential]] is related to the [[Helmholtz free energy]] (logarithm of the canonical partition function), <math>F\,</math>, in the following way:<ref name="dill"/>

<math display="block"> G = F + PV. </math>

==Applications==

*Constant-pressure simulations are useful for determining the [[equation of state]] of a pure system. Monte Carlo simulations using the <math>NpT</math>-ensemble are particularly useful for determining the equation of state of fluids at pressures of around 1 atm, where they can achieve accurate results with much less computational time than other ensembles.<ref name="frenkel"/>
*Zero-pressure <math>NpT</math>-ensemble simulations provide a quick way of estimating vapor-liquid coexistence curves in mixed-phase systems.<ref name="frenkel"/>
*<math>NpT</math>-ensemble Monte Carlo simulations have been applied to study the [[excess property|excess properties]]<ref name="mcdonald">{{cite journal |last1=McDonald |first1= I. R. |date= 1972|title= <math>NpT</math>-ensemble Monte Carlo calculations for binary liquid mixtures|journal= [[Molecular Physics (journal)|Molecular Physics]] |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=41–58 |doi=10.1080/00268977200100031|bibcode= 1972MolPh..23...41M }}</ref> and equations of state <ref name="wood">{{cite journal |last1=Wood |first1= W. W. |date= 1970|title= <math>NpT</math>-Ensemble Monte Carlo Calculations for the Hard Disk Fluid|journal= Journal of Chemical Physics |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=729–741 |doi=10.1063/1.1673047 |bibcode= 1970JChPh..52..729W }}</ref> of various models of fluid mixtures.
*The <math>NpT</math>-ensemble is also useful in [[molecular dynamics]] simulations, e.g. to model the behavior of water at ambient conditions.<ref name="schmidt">{{cite journal |last1=Schmidt |first1= Jochen |last2=VandeVondele |first2= Joost |last3=Kuo |first3= I. F. William |last4=Sebastiani |first4= Daniel |last5=Siepmann |first5= J. Ilja |last6=Hutter |first6= Jürg |last7=Mundy |first7= Christopher J. |date= 2009|title= Isobaric-Isothermal Molecular Dynamics Simulations Utilizing Density Functional Theory:An Assessment of the Structure and Density of Water at Near-Ambient Conditions |journal= Journal of Physical Chemistry B |volume=113 |issue=35 |pages=11959–11964 |doi=10.1021/jp901990u|pmid= 19663399 |osti= 980890 }}</ref>
